s1: Namaskaram. A teacher from IIT, who also trained for years in the Vedas, stood on a stage and answered one question: why study the scriptures in the age of AI? I will decode every Sanskrit line he quoted, word by word, root by root. Light the diya, and let us begin.
sg: Before we go further, a map. In English, little words like by, from and to show how a noun relates to the action. Sanskrit puts that into the ending of the word itself, called its case. Tap each role around the action, then build a sentence and see why eight cases are enough.
s2: He began in Sanskrit, then begged pardon for switching to English. Notice the humility. He has walked two paths at once: the gurukula and the IIT. Tap the words below, and meet your first roots: gir, vach, and yach. Roots are the seeds from which Sanskrit words grow.
s3: His boldest claim: studying the shastras is not only for India. It is non-negotiable for every person. He quoted Manu: from the foremost teachers of this land, let all people on earth learn their conduct. Build the verse yourself, and see how the grammar fits together.
s4: Level one: the intellect. He says, give me someone trained in Nyaya, logic, for twelve years, and I can teach them quantum physics in one. This is his experience, not a study. The idea is buddhi vaishadya, clarity of mind. Slide the years, and see what clarity means.
s5: Now his surprising example: the Transformer, the engine behind modern AI. Each word's meaning is blended from the words around it. He links this to an old idea, that words get their meaning in relation to each other. Treat it as a resemblance, not a proof. Tap a word.
s6: Then comes his warning. Do not hunt for science in the shastras. Plant a field for the grain, and straw comes along. Plant for the straw alone, and you only get straw. For him, today's science is the by-product, not the harvest. Try both choices.
s7: Level two: society. We now face something powerful, which he calls deva and danava, and we do not know how to handle it. He turns to a famous line: helping others brings merit, harming others brings sin. Sort these algorithm decisions, and notice how old the question is.
s8: Why do we build harmful things at all? He says, because contentment is gone. Today's success metric is produce more, consume more. The scriptures ask for santosha, contentment with what comes. Move the slider toward more, then toward enough, and watch the two meters.
s9: Level three: the self. He quotes the Bhagavata: mukti, liberation, is leaving behind everything other than yourself, and standing in your own true nature. It is not escape. It is arrival. Peel the layers one by one, and see what is left.
s10: Here is a story he loves. Maitreyi asks her husband Yajnavalkya: if I owned the whole earth, would I be immortal? No, he says. Wealth gives no hope of that. And her reply is, to him, the most beautiful line he has read. Help her ask it.
s11: Nachiketa meets Yama, who offers him wealth, long life, chariots, song and dance. The boy says: all life is short anyway. The speaker, a mathematician, adds: take the biggest number you can imagine, and it still shrinks to nothing against eternity. Slide the years, and see.
s12: A yaksha asks Yudhishthira: what is the greatest wonder? His answer: day after day, beings go to Yama's abode, yet the rest wish to stay forever. The speaker says we plan every day as though we will never leave. Arrange the lines, then answer as Yudhishthira.
s13: He sets this against stay hungry, stay foolish, and against colonies on Mars. Nachiketa would ask: will going to Mars make me immortal? The scriptures, he says, offer the biggest ambition of all: lasting happiness, called mumuksha. Follow the chain of whys, then see what he asks of his students.
s14: You have decoded every passage. Now see how a few roots connect them. Explore the word lab, take the quiz to earn the rank of Acharya, and copy the decoder card to keep. Study first, he says, and then debate.
